lesson.title: break: Exiting a Loop Before It's Done
lesson.summary: The break statement immediately ends the nearest enclosing loop, letting a program stop repeating the moment it finds what it needs instead of grinding through every remaining pass.
lesson.body:
Normally, a loop keeps running until its natural stopping point: a for loop runs out of items, or a while loop's condition becomes False. The break statement overrides that entirely. The moment Python executes break, it exits the loop immediately, skipping any remaining lines in the current body and skipping any remaining iterations completely, jumping straight to the first statement written after the loop.

This is especially useful for searching, where continuing to check items after you have already found the one you wanted would just waste time and computation for no benefit, particularly once the collection being searched grows large. Consider:
numbers = [5, 12, 8, 19, 3]
target = 8
for n in numbers:
    print("Checking", n)
    if n == target:
        print("Found it!")
        break
Trace it pass by pass carefully. n is 5: it prints "Checking 5", and 5 == 8 is False, so nothing else happens this pass. n is 12: it prints "Checking 12", and 12 == 8 is False. n is 8: it prints "Checking 8", and now 8 == 8 is True, so "Found it!" is printed, and then break runs, ending the loop right there on the spot. Crucially, 19 and 3 are never checked at all, the loop does not continue on to them, because break cut the whole process off as soon as the target was located.

break works in while loops exactly the same way it does in for loops, and combining while True with a break inside an if, as shown when discussing infinite loops, is one of the most common patterns in real code: a loop that would otherwise run forever, deliberately given a specific, well-defined exit condition instead of a condition checked automatically at the top. In both loop forms, break behaves identically: it does not care whether the loop was going to stop on its own eventually, it simply cuts execution off the instant it runs.

One subtlety worth knowing ahead of nested loops: break only exits the loop it is directly written inside, and nothing further out than that. If a break statement sits inside an inner loop that is itself sitting inside an outer loop, it ends only the inner loop for that pass, and the outer loop simply continues on to its own next pass as usual, entirely unaffected by what happened inside.

It also helps to notice what break skips over entirely: the else clause that Python allows on both for and while loops, which runs only if the loop completed every pass without ever hitting a break. That behavior is a direct consequence of what break does, cutting the loop off before it would otherwise reach that natural, unbroken end.

Stepping back, break is best understood as a deliberate exception to the general rule that loops keep going until their built-in stopping condition is met on its own. It gives you explicit, immediate control to say "stop right now," which is exactly what searching, matching, and plenty of other real, practical tasks actually need in order to run efficiently rather than wastefully.
